rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their property indicated : (Any two)
(i) Acetaldehyde, Benzaldehyde, Acetophenone, Acetone (Reactivity towards HCN)
(ii) \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCOOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH}\) (Acidic strength)
(iii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) (Boiling point)
rows.solution:
(i) Increasing reactivity towards hydrogen cyanide:
ACETOPHENONE < BENZALDEHYDE < ACETONE < ACETALDEHYDE

Nucleophilic addition begins with cyanide attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded. Both ALKYL and ARYL groups do this, but a phenyl group does it far more strongly — it DELOCALISES the carbonyl \(\pi\) system into the ring, relieving the carbon of positive charge, and the flat ring is bulky besides.

So the two AROMATIC compounds come first, acetophenone below benzaldehyde because it has a methyl group as well as the ring. Then the two ALIPHATIC ones, acetone with two alkyl groups below acetaldehyde with one.

(ii) Increasing acidic strength:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCOOH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH}\)

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate anion. BROMINE withdraws electron density and stabilises it; the ISOPROPYL group releases density and destabilises it, so the unbrominated acid is weakest.

Between the two brominated acids the DISTANCE decides. The inductive effect falls off sharply along a chain, so bromine on the \(\alpha\) carbon — next to the carboxyl — is far more effective than bromine on the \(\beta\) carbon, one place further away.

(iii) Increasing boiling point:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} < \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

All three are of comparable molar mass, so the order is set by INTERMOLECULAR FORCES. Ethanal has a polar carbonyl but no \(\mathrm{O-H}\), so only dipole-dipole attraction (293 K). Ethanol has one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) and hydrogen bonds in an open chain (351 K). Ethanoic acid forms TWO hydrogen bonds between each pair of molecules, locking them into a DIMER (391 K).

rows.stem: In a plot of \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) against the square root of concentration (\(\mathrm{C}^{1/2}\)) for strong and weak electrolyte, the value of limiting molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte cannot be obtained graphically. Suggest a way to obtain this value. Also state the related law, if any.
rows.solution:
Use KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW OF INDEPENDENT MIGRATION OF IONS.

WHY THE GRAPH FAILS. For a STRONG electrolyte, \(\Lambda_m\) plotted against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is nearly a straight line, because full dissociation means the only thing changing with dilution is how much the ions interfere with one another. Extrapolating that line to zero concentration gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) directly.

For a WEAK electrolyte the curve rises steeply near infinite dilution, because the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION itself is increasing. It runs almost PARALLEL to the vertical axis and never gives an intercept, so there is nothing to extrapolate.

THE WAY ROUND IT: build the value up from the IONS instead of measuring it for the compound.

KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the SUM of the individual contributions of its cation and its anion, each counted as often as the formula unit provides it:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \nu_+\lambda_+^{\circ} + \nu_-\lambda_-^{\circ}\)

At infinite dilution each ion moves entirely INDEPENDENTLY of the other, which is what makes the simple sum valid. The individual ionic values come from STRONG electrolytes, whose graphs do extrapolate — so, for example,
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) + \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) - \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write reasons for the following statements :
(i) Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(ii) Oxidation of aldehydes is easier than that of ketones.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the carboxyl group is strongly DEACTIVATING, and because it bonds to the CATALYST.

A Friedel-Crafts reaction attacks the ring with an electrophile, so it needs a ring rich in electrons. The \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group WITHDRAWS electron density, both inductively and by resonance, leaving the ring too electron-poor to attack an electrophile.

The catalyst is the second obstacle. Anhydrous aluminium chloride is a Lewis acid, and it coordinates to the carboxyl group's oxygen — so the catalyst is tied up, and the carboxyl group, now carrying a positive charge, deactivates the ring further still.

(ii) Because oxidising an aldehyde breaks a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond, whereas oxidising a ketone must break a \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond.

An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon carries a HYDROGEN. Oxidation simply replaces it by a hydroxyl, and the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond is comparatively weak — so even Tollens' or Fehling's reagent, both mild, will do it.

A ketone's carbonyl carbon carries no hydrogen, being flanked by two carbons, so oxidation must CLEAVE the carbon skeleton. That needs a powerful oxidising agent and drastic conditions, and gives a mixture of shorter acids.

rows.stem:
Write reasons for the following :
(i) Ethylamine is soluble in water whereas aniline is insoluble.
(ii) Amino group is o- and p-directing in aromatic electrophilic substitution reactions, but aniline on nitration gives a substantial amount of m-nitroaniline.
(iii) Amines behave as nucleophiles.
rows.solution:
(i) Because ethylamine HYDROGEN BONDS to water readily while aniline does not.

Both have an \(\mathrm{N-H}\) group, so both can in principle hydrogen bond. What differs is the rest of the molecule. Ethylamine's ethyl group is small, so the hydrogen bonding dominates and the amine is freely soluble.

Aniline carries a large BENZENE RING, a bulky hydrocarbon portion with no affinity for water at all. It gets in the way of the hydrogen bonding and dominates the molecule, so aniline is only sparingly soluble.

(ii) Because nitration is carried out in a STRONGLY ACIDIC medium, in which aniline is largely PROTONATED.

The nitrating mixture converts aniline to the ANILINIUM ion, and \(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{N}}\mathrm{H_3}\) has no lone pair to donate and carries a positive charge — so it WITHDRAWS density powerfully and becomes META directing, like a nitro group.

Two species then react in parallel: the small amount of free aniline giving ortho and para products, and the protonated form giving meta. The result is about 47% meta.

(iii) Because the nitrogen carries a LONE PAIR of electrons.

A nucleophile is a species that DONATES an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre, and an amine's nitrogen has one available. That single fact accounts for the whole of amine chemistry: alkylation with alkyl halides, acylation with acyl chlorides, salt formation with acids, and coordination to metal ions as a ligand.

The same lone pair also makes amines BASES — a base donates its pair to a proton, a nucleophile to a carbon, and the two behaviours are one property seen at two different targets.

rows.stem:
How will you carry out the following conversions :
(i) Nitrobenzene to Aniline
(ii) Ethanamide to Methanamine
(iii) Ethanenitrile to Ethanamine
rows.solution:
(i) NITROBENZENE TO ANILINE — reduce the nitro group with a metal and acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Tin with hydrochloric acid does the same job; catalytic hydrogenation over nickel or palladium is the alternative. In the acid medium the amine forms as its salt, and alkali is added at the end to liberate the free amine.

(ii) ETHANAMIDE TO METHANAMINE — count the carbons: TWO in, ONE out, so a carbon must be LOST, and that is the signature of the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The lost carbon is the CARBONYL carbon, leaving as carbonate.

(iii) ETHANENITRILE TO ETHANAMINE — count again: TWO in, TWO out, so nothing is lost and the nitrile is simply REDUCED:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\)

Sodium in ethanol does the same. Counting carbons is what separates this from the previous conversion: one loses a carbon, the other does not.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the electronic configuration of \(d^5\) on the basis of crystal field splitting theory if \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\).
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) is weakly paramagnetic whereas \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) is diamagnetic. Give reason to support this statement.
[Atomic no. : Fe = 26]
(iii) Write the number of ions produced from the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_2}\) in solution.
rows.solution:
(i) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) — a WEAK FIELD — promotion is cheaper, so the electrons spread out as widely as they can, one to each of the five orbitals. All FIVE are unpaired: a HIGH SPIN complex with \(\mu = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M.

(ii) Because the two differ by ONE ELECTRON, and that electron is the last unpaired one.

Iron is atomic number 26. In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) iron is \(+3\), that is \(3d^5\); in \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) it is \(+2\), that is \(3d^6\).

CYANIDE is a STRONG field ligand in both, pairing the electrons into the lower three orbitals. Five electrons give \(t_{2g}^5\) — two pairs and ONE UNPAIRED electron, so the complex is WEAKLY paramagnetic, \(\mu = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M. Six electrons give \(t_{2g}^6\) — three pairs and NONE left over, so that complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

(iii) THREE ions. Only what sits outside the brackets ionises:
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-}\)

One complex cation plus two chlorides. The six ammines are LIGANDS and stay with the cobalt.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the spin only magnetic moment of the complex \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\). (Atomic no. of Co = 27)
(ii) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[CrCl_2(H_2O)_4]Cl}\)
(iii) Which out of the two complexes is more stable and why ?
\(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\)
rows.solution:
(i) Cobalt is 27, and six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so cobalt is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\).

FLUORIDE is a WEAK field ligand and cannot force pairing, so the six electrons spread out as far as Hund's rule allows — one pair and FOUR unpaired:
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24}\)

\(\mu = 4{\cdot}90\ \mathrm{B.M.}\)

With a strong field ligand such as ammonia the same ion would pair all six electrons and the moment would be zero.

(ii) The two chlorido ligands give \(-2\), the four aqua ligands are neutral, and one chloride sits outside — so chromium must be \(+3\). Ligands are named in ALPHABETICAL order, "aqua" before "chlorido":
TETRAAQUADICHLORIDOCHROMIUM(III) CHLORIDE

(iii) \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\) is the more stable, because of the CHELATE EFFECT.

The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE, binding the iron through two oxygens at once and closing a five-membered ring; three of them close three rings. Water is monodentate and closes none.

Two reasons: once one donor atom has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily; and releasing a chelating ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Which ion amongst the following is colourless and why ?
\(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\)
(Atomic number of Ti = 22, Cr = 24, V = 23)
(ii) Why is \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) much more resistant than \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) towards oxidation ?
(iii) Highest oxidation state of a metal is shown in its oxide or fluoride only. Justify the statement.
rows.solution:
(i) \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\) is colourless.

Work out the configurations. Titanium is 22, so \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\) is \(3d^0\); vanadium is 23, so \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) is \(3d^2\); chromium is 24, so \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\).

Colour arises from a D-D TRANSITION, an electron absorbing visible light and jumping from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper. Titanium(IV) has NO d electron at all — it has the argon configuration — so no such jump is possible. The other two have electrons available and are coloured, vanadium(III) green and chromium(III) violet.

(ii) Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ALREADY HAS the stable half-filled configuration, while \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) reaches it by being oxidised.

Manganese(II) is \(3d^5\) — every orbital singly occupied, spins parallel, an arrangement of unusual stability. Oxidising it to \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) would DESTROY that, giving \(3d^4\), so it resists.

Iron(II) is \(3d^6\), one electron beyond the stable set. Losing that electron gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which IS \(3d^5\), so iron(II) is oxidised readily — which is why a solution of an iron(II) salt turns yellow-brown in air.

(iii) Because OXYGEN and FLUORINE alone can stabilise a metal in so high a state.

Reaching the highest oxidation state means stripping the metal of every available electron, leaving a very small, very highly charged centre. Holding it requires a partner that is itself SMALL and HIGHLY ELECTRONEGATIVE, and fluorine and oxygen are the two extremes of both.

Oxygen has a further advantage: it can form MULTIPLE BONDS to the metal, using its \(p\) orbitals, and so donate more electron density than fluorine can. That is why \(+7\) appears in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) and \(+6\) in \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\), while no chloride or bromide of manganese(VII) exists — the halogen would simply be oxidised instead.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: A compound 'A' (\(\mathrm{C_2H_4O}\)) on oxidation gives 'B' (\(\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}\)). 'A' undergoes Iodoform reaction to give yellow precipitate and reacts with HCN to form the compound 'C'. 'C' on hydrolysis gives 2-hydroxypropanoic acid. Identify the compounds 'A', 'B' and 'C'. Write down equations for the reactions involved.
rows.solution:
Take the clues in order.

'A' has the formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O}\) and gives the IODOFORM reaction, so it has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group; with only two carbons, it must be an aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal

Oxidation gives \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}\), one oxygen more:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), ethanoic acid
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + [\mathrm{O}] \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

Hydrogen cyanide ADDS across the carbonyl group, giving the cyanohydrin with THREE carbons:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN}\), 2-hydroxypropanenitrile
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN}\)

Hydrolysis of the nitrile group gives the acid, which confirms the identification:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)COOH} + \mathrm{NH_3}\)

That product is 2-HYDROXYPROPANOIC ACID — lactic acid — exactly as the question states, so the chain of identifications closes.

The IODOFORM reaction itself:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CHI_3}\downarrow + \mathrm{HCOONa} + 3\mathrm{NaI} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.stem:
Observe the given figure and answer the following questions :
(i) Write the expression for adsorption of gases on solids in the form of an equation.
(ii) What is the slope of the graph ?
(iii) What does the intercept of the line represent ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem is 'Observe the given figure' and sub-parts (ii) and (iii) ask for the slope and the intercept of THAT plot; the text names no axis and no quantity, so the row is unanswerable without the crop. The printed graph is a straight line rising to the right, plotted with y-axis labelled 'Log x/m' (x over m, written as a fraction, with an up arrow) and x-axis labelled 'Log p' with a right arrow, origin marked O. The line is extrapolated leftwards as a DASHED segment to a positive intercept on the y-axis, which is marked by a brace. A right triangle is drawn on the line with its angle at the line labelled Q, its horizontal side labelled a and its vertical side labelled b. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The graph plots \(\log(x/m)\) against \(\log p\) and gives a STRAIGHT LINE — which is the logarithmic form of the FREUNDLICH ADSORPTION ISOTHERM.

(i) THE EQUATION. The isotherm relates the mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent to the pressure:
\(\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,p^{1/n}\) where \(n > 1\)

Here \(x\) is the mass of gas adsorbed, \(m\) the mass of the adsorbent, \(p\) the pressure, and \(k\) and \(n\) are constants for a given adsorbent and gas at a given temperature.

Taking logarithms of both sides gives the straight line the figure shows:
\(\log\dfrac{x}{m} = \log k + \dfrac{1}{n}\log p\)

(ii) THE SLOPE is \(\dfrac{1}{n}\) — the ratio \(b/a\) marked on the figure, that is \(\tan \mathrm{Q}\).

(iii) THE INTERCEPT on the vertical axis is \(\log k\), the value of \(\log(x/m)\) where \(\log p = 0\).

Comparing the equation with \(y = mx + c\) shows both at once: the coefficient of \(\log p\) is the slope, and the constant term is the intercept.

rows.stem:
Write equations involved in the following reactions :
(i) Ethanamine reacts with acetyl chloride.
(ii) Aniline reacts with bromine water at room temperature.
(iii) Aniline reacts with chloroform and ethanolic potassium hydroxide.
rows.solution:
(i) ACYLATION. The amine's lone pair attacks the acyl chloride, and a base is present to absorb the hydrogen chloride and drive the reaction forward:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CH_3COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{base}} \mathrm{C_2H_5NHCOCH_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product is N-ethylethanamide. Note that the amide nitrogen is far LESS basic than the amine's was, its lone pair now shared with the carbonyl group — which is exactly why acylation is used to protect an amino group.

(ii) BROMINATION. The amino group is so strongly activating that bromine water brominates all three of the activated positions at once, with no way to stop at one:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3NH_2} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

The product is 2,4,6-TRIBROMOANILINE, which separates as a white precipitate.

(iii) CARBYLAMINE REACTION — a test for primary amines, giving an isocyanide of exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is PHENYL ISOCYANIDE. Forming it requires the nitrogen to give up BOTH of its hydrogens, so secondary and tertiary amines do not respond.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the IUPAC name for the following organic compound :
\((\mathrm{CH_3CH_2})_2\mathrm{NCH_3}\)
(ii) Write the equations for the following :
(I) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
(II) Hoffmann bromamide degradation
rows.solution:
(i) The nitrogen carries THREE alkyl groups — two ethyls and a methyl — so the compound is a tertiary amine. The LONGEST chain attached to the nitrogen becomes the parent, and the other two groups are named as N-substituents in alphabetical order:
N-ETHYL-N-METHYLETHANAMINE

(ii)(I) GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS, in three steps:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{R{-}X}} \text{N-alkylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \text{sodium phthalate}\)

Potassium hydroxide removes the imide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, made acidic by the two flanking carbonyls; the anion then displaces halide in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) step; alkaline hydrolysis frees the amine. The product is a PURE PRIMARY amine, which is the point of the method — and it fails for aromatic amines, an aryl halide not undergoing that substitution.

(II) HOFFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION gives a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The lost carbon is the CARBONYL carbon, leaving as carbonate, while the alkyl group migrates from that carbon to the nitrogen.

rows.stem:
Write the Nernst equation and calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Cr} \,|\, \mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \,\|\, \mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \,|\, \mathrm{Fe}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = -\,0{\cdot}75\ \mathrm{V}\)
\(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = -\,0{\cdot}45\ \mathrm{V}\)
(log 10 = 1)
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: chromium is on the LEFT and so is the anode, oxidised; iron(II) is reduced at the right.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = -0{\cdot}45 - (-0{\cdot}75) = 0{\cdot}30\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing the electrons gives \(2\mathrm{Cr} + 3\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Fe}\), so \(n = 6\). Solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}30 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log\dfrac{(0{\cdot}1)^2}{(0{\cdot}01)^3} = 0{\cdot}30 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log\dfrac{10^{-2}}{10^{-6}}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}30 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log 10^{4} = 0{\cdot}30 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059 \times 4}{6}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}30 - 0{\cdot}0393\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}2607\ \mathrm{V}\), about \(0{\cdot}26\) V

The EXPONENTS are what the question tests: each concentration is raised to its coefficient in the balanced equation, so the quotient is \(10^{-2}/10^{-6}\), not \(10^{-1}/10^{-2}\).

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Silver atom has completely filled d-orbitals in its ground state, it is still considered to be a transition element. Justify the statement.
(ii) Why are \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}}\) values of Mn and Zn more negative than expected ?
(iii) Why do transition metals form alloys ?
rows.solution:
(i) Because \(\mathrm{Ag^{2+}}\) has a PARTLY FILLED d subshell.

The definition of a transition element allows TWO routes in: a partly filled d subshell in the neutral ATOM, or in at least one of its stable IONS. Silver fails the first test — the atom is \([\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{10} 5s^1\) — but passes the second, since \(\mathrm{Ag^{2+}}\) is \(4d^9\).

Copper is the exactly analogous case in the 3d series: \(3d^{10}\) as the atom, \(3d^9\) as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\).

(ii) Because their \(+2\) IONS are exceptionally stable, and stability of the ion drives the metal to form it.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\), an exactly HALF-FILLED subshell; \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\), COMPLETELY FILLED. Both arrangements are unusually stable, so in each case the metal gives up its two electrons more readily than its neighbours do.

A metal easily oxidised has a more NEGATIVE reduction potential, so both values fall below what the general trend across the series would predict.

(iii) Because their ATOMIC RADII are very similar.

Across the transition series the radii differ by only a few picometres, so one metal's atoms can replace another's in the crystal lattice without disturbing the structure. Such SUBSTITUTIONAL alloys form readily, and often have properties — hardness, corrosion resistance — better than either component. Brass, bronze and stainless steel are the familiar examples.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Answer the following questions on the basis of the figure given below :
(i) Which element in 3d series has lowest enthalpy of atomisation ?
(ii) Why do metals of the second and third series have greater enthalpies of atomisation ?
(iii) Why are enthalpies of atomisation of transition metals quite high ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem is 'Answer the following questions on the basis of the figure given below' and sub-part (i) asks which 3d-series element has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation, which is read off the curve; the text supplies no data. The printed graph plots three line curves against a y-axis labelled 'delta-a H (circled-minus superscript) / kJ mol^-1' scaled 0 to 900 in steps of 100, and an x-axis labelled 'Atomic number' with a right arrow and no tick labels. The three curves are labelled by arrows as Series 1 (lowest, peaking near 500), Series 2 (middle, peaking near 720) and Series 3 (highest, peaking near 840); all three fall steeply at the right-hand end. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
(i) ZINC has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the 3d series.

Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\) — every d electron PAIRED and held tightly to its own atom — so only the two \(4s\) electrons contribute to the metallic bond. With the weakest bond in the series it has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation, and the lowest melting and boiling points; mercury below it is liquid at room temperature.

(ii) Because the \(4d\) and \(5d\) orbitals are LARGER and more DIFFUSE, so they overlap more effectively between neighbouring atoms.

Metal-metal bonding depends on how well the d orbitals of adjacent atoms overlap, and the compact \(3d\) orbitals of the first series do this relatively poorly. The more extended \(4d\) and \(5d\) orbitals reach further and overlap better, giving stronger bonds and higher enthalpies of atomisation — which is why tungsten, in the 5d series, has the highest melting point of any metal.

(iii) Because a LARGE NUMBER OF UNPAIRED d ELECTRONS take part in the metallic bond.

In a main-group metal only the outermost \(s\) and \(p\) electrons contribute. In a transition metal the unpaired d electrons contribute as well, so far more electrons hold the lattice together and far more energy is needed to pull an atom out of it.

The trend within a series follows directly: the more unpaired d electrons, the higher the value. Chromium, with six, is among the highest; zinc, with none, the lowest.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Calculate the overall order of a reaction which has the following rate expression :
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{1/2}\,[\mathrm{B}]^{3/2}\)
rows.context: The rate law for a chemical reaction relates the reaction rate with the concentrations or partial pressures of the reactants. For a general reaction aA + bB \(\rightarrow\) C with no intermediate steps in its reaction mechanism, meaning that it is an elementary reaction, the rate law is given by \(r = k[\mathrm{A}]^{x}[\mathrm{B}]^{y}\), where [A] and [B] express the concentrations of A and B in moles per litre. Exponents x and y vary for each reaction and are determined experimentally. The value of k varies with conditions that affect reaction rate, such as temperature, pressure, surface area, etc. The sum of these exponents is known as overall reaction order. A zero order reaction has a constant rate that is independent of the concentration of the reactants. A first order reaction depends on the concentration of only one reactant. A reaction is said to be second order when the overall order is two. Once we have determined the order of the reaction, we can go back and plug in one set of our initial values and solve for k.
rows.solution:
The OVERALL ORDER is the sum of the exponents in the rate law:
\(\text{Order} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2} = 2\)

The individual orders are FRACTIONAL, and the overall order comes out a whole number only by coincidence of the halves adding.

What the fractions tell us is that the reaction is COMPLEX — it goes through a sequence of elementary steps rather than a single collision, and the measured order reflects the slowest of them. Order is an experimental quantity and need not be a whole number, need not be positive, and need not match the coefficients in any balanced equation.

MOLECULARITY, by contrast, counts colliding species in a single elementary step and must be a whole number of at least 1.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: What is the effect of temperature on rate of reaction ?
rows.context: The rate law for a chemical reaction relates the reaction rate with the concentrations or partial pressures of the reactants. For a general reaction aA + bB \(\rightarrow\) C with no intermediate steps in its reaction mechanism, meaning that it is an elementary reaction, the rate law is given by \(r = k[\mathrm{A}]^{x}[\mathrm{B}]^{y}\), where [A] and [B] express the concentrations of A and B in moles per litre. Exponents x and y vary for each reaction and are determined experimentally. The value of k varies with conditions that affect reaction rate, such as temperature, pressure, surface area, etc. The sum of these exponents is known as overall reaction order. A zero order reaction has a constant rate that is independent of the concentration of the reactants. A first order reaction depends on the concentration of only one reactant. A reaction is said to be second order when the overall order is two. Once we have determined the order of the reaction, we can go back and plug in one set of our initial values and solve for k.
rows.solution:
The rate INCREASES with temperature.

The Arrhenius equation gives \(k = \mathrm{A}e^{-E_a/\mathrm{RT}}\). Raising \(\mathrm{T}\) makes the exponent less negative, so the exponential term grows and the rate constant with it.

The reason is not chiefly that the molecules collide more often — that effect is small. It is that a far larger FRACTION of the collisions now carry at least the ACTIVATION ENERGY, so a far larger fraction of them are effective. Near room temperature a rise of ten degrees roughly DOUBLES the rate for a typical reaction.

Note what does NOT change: the activation energy itself, which is fixed by the nature of the reactants. Only a CATALYST alters that, by offering a different path with a lower barrier.

rows.stem: What is meant by rate of a reaction ?
rows.context: The rate law for a chemical reaction relates the reaction rate with the concentrations or partial pressures of the reactants. For a general reaction aA + bB \(\rightarrow\) C with no intermediate steps in its reaction mechanism, meaning that it is an elementary reaction, the rate law is given by \(r = k[\mathrm{A}]^{x}[\mathrm{B}]^{y}\), where [A] and [B] express the concentrations of A and B in moles per litre. Exponents x and y vary for each reaction and are determined experimentally. The value of k varies with conditions that affect reaction rate, such as temperature, pressure, surface area, etc. The sum of these exponents is known as overall reaction order. A zero order reaction has a constant rate that is independent of the concentration of the reactants. A first order reaction depends on the concentration of only one reactant. A reaction is said to be second order when the overall order is two. Once we have determined the order of the reaction, we can go back and plug in one set of our initial values and solve for k.
rows.solution:
The RATE OF A REACTION is the change in the concentration of a reactant or a product per unit time — the DECREASE in the concentration of a reactant, or the INCREASE in that of a product:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{\Delta[\text{Reactant}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{\Delta[\text{Product}]}{\Delta t}\)

The MINUS sign is not cosmetic: a reactant's concentration falls, so \(\Delta[\mathrm{R}]\) is negative, and the sign makes the rate positive as a rate must be.

Where the coefficients are not all 1, each species' own rate is divided by its coefficient, so that one number describes the whole reaction:
for \(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \longrightarrow c\mathrm{C}\), \(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{a}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{A}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{C}]}{\Delta t}\)

Its usual units are \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

rows.stem: A first order reaction takes \(77{\cdot}78\) minutes for 50% completion. Calculate the time required for 30% completion of this reaction. (log 10 = 1, log 7 = \(0{\cdot}8450\))
rows.context: The rate law for a chemical reaction relates the reaction rate with the concentrations or partial pressures of the reactants. For a general reaction aA + bB \(\rightarrow\) C with no intermediate steps in its reaction mechanism, meaning that it is an elementary reaction, the rate law is given by \(r = k[\mathrm{A}]^{x}[\mathrm{B}]^{y}\), where [A] and [B] express the concentrations of A and B in moles per litre. Exponents x and y vary for each reaction and are determined experimentally. The value of k varies with conditions that affect reaction rate, such as temperature, pressure, surface area, etc. The sum of these exponents is known as overall reaction order. A zero order reaction has a constant rate that is independent of the concentration of the reactants. A first order reaction depends on the concentration of only one reactant. A reaction is said to be second order when the overall order is two. Once we have determined the order of the reaction, we can go back and plug in one set of our initial values and solve for k.
rows.solution:
The reaction is FIRST ORDER, and "50% completion" IS the half-life:
\(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{77{\cdot}78} = 0{\cdot}008909\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

For 30% completion, 70% REMAINS — so taking the initial amount as 100, the amount left is 70:
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{70} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{0{\cdot}008909}\,(\log 10 - \log 7)\)
\(= 258{\cdot}50 \times (1 - 0{\cdot}8450) = 258{\cdot}50 \times 0{\cdot}155\)

\(t = 40{\cdot}06\ \mathrm{min}\)

The check is immediate: 30% completion is LESS than 50%, so the time must be less than the half-life of 77.78 minutes — and 40 minutes is comfortably under it.

The commonest error is to put 30 rather than 70 into the ratio. The equation needs the amount REMAINING, not the amount consumed.

rows.stem:
A first order reaction has a rate constant \(1 \times 10^{-3}\) per sec. How long will 5 g of this reactant take to reduce to 3 g ?
(log 3 = \(0{\cdot}4771\); log 5 = \(0{\cdot}6990\))
rows.context: The rate law for a chemical reaction relates the reaction rate with the concentrations or partial pressures of the reactants. For a general reaction aA + bB \(\rightarrow\) C with no intermediate steps in its reaction mechanism, meaning that it is an elementary reaction, the rate law is given by \(r = k[\mathrm{A}]^{x}[\mathrm{B}]^{y}\), where [A] and [B] express the concentrations of A and B in moles per litre. Exponents x and y vary for each reaction and are determined experimentally. The value of k varies with conditions that affect reaction rate, such as temperature, pressure, surface area, etc. The sum of these exponents is known as overall reaction order. A zero order reaction has a constant rate that is independent of the concentration of the reactants. A first order reaction depends on the concentration of only one reactant. A reaction is said to be second order when the overall order is two. Once we have determined the order of the reaction, we can go back and plug in one set of our initial values and solve for k.
rows.solution:
The reaction is FIRST ORDER, so the integrated rate law can be used with MASSES directly — the units cancel in the ratio:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Rearranging for the time, with 5 g falling to 3 g:
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{1 \times 10^{-3}}\log\dfrac{5}{3} = 2{\cdot}303 \times 10^{3}\,(\log 5 - \log 3)\)
\(= 2303 \times (0{\cdot}6990 - 0{\cdot}4771) = 2303 \times 0{\cdot}2219\)

\(t = 511\ \mathrm{s}\), about eight and a half minutes

A rough check: the half-life is \(0{\cdot}693/10^{-3} = 693\) s, and 5 g has not yet fallen to half — 2.5 g would be half — so the time must be somewhat LESS than 693 s, as 511 s is.
